name: Tzeltal
sweep_summary: The one sweep item, Shklovsky 2011 'Petalcingo Tseltal intonational prosody' (FAMLi I, MITWPL 63: 209-220), is a print-only paid volume (MITWPL catalog page fetched sources; no open copy on lingbuzz, IA Scholar, BASE, Wayback; bibliographic APIs rate-limited); by its title and the way Shklovsky 2012 and DiCanio & Bennett 2018 cite it, it is about boundary tones (H% on declaratives/wh-questions, L% on polar questions), not word-stress placement; medium priority. Three open sources were newly fetched sources from archive.org and read: Gerdel 1974 'Tzeltal (Mayan) phonemes' section 1.4 (first-hand: final stress on the stress/pause group, secondary initial stress, Spanish penult loans unshifted), the Stanford Phonology Archive 1979 entry summarizing Kaufman 1971 (root-morpheme stress, affixes unstressed, primary stress only phrase-finally; this is the source of the 'word-initial' counter-claim, and it contradicts a word-level fixed-final coding), and the Spanish original of Smith's manual (same 'always last syllable' statement); the 1957 Chicago 'El Tzeltal Hablado' course is silent. Polian 2013 (on file under tzel1255) remains the best first-hand statement: fixed final accent at the phonological-phrase level, realized by F0 rise and lengthening, with listed loan exceptions and root-initial emphatic lengthening; it should replace the Wikipedia/Smith citation and the domain should be coded PHRASE, with Kaufman 1971 (still unread, archive.org lending only) as the high-priority acquisition. Files and md5s are logged in

new_statements.quote: El tseltal es una lengua de acento fijo (Kager, 2007), y por lo mismo no presenta un acento léxicamente contrastivo como el español. El acento recae sobre la última sílaba de las frases fonológicas, y en particular al final del enunciado. [...] El acento final no concierne propiamente las palabras, sino las frases fonológicas, que se pueden caracterizar aproximativamente como los constituyentes prosódicos que agrupan un núcleo léxico y todos sus satélites [...] si una palabra viene seguida de clíticos, estos se integran a la misma frase fonológica que la palabra anterior y pueden por lo tanto llevar el acento final
new_statements.translation: Tseltal is a fixed-accent language (Kager 2007), and so has no lexically contrastive accent as Spanish does. The accent falls on the last syllable of phonological phrases, and in particular at the end of the utterance. [...] The final accent does not properly concern words but phonological phrases, which can be roughly characterized as the prosodic constituents grouping a lexical head and all its satellites [...] if a word is followed by clitics, these join the same phonological phrase as the preceding word and can therefore carry the final accent
new_statements.citation: Polian, Gilles (2013). Gramática del tseltal de Oxchuc, Tomo I. México: CIESAS (Publicaciones de la Casa Chata). Section 3.2 'Acento y prosodia', pp. 85-87 (and 3.8.10, p. 123).
new_statements.reading: Fixed final accent, but the domain is the phonological phrase (utterance-final above all), realized by an F0 rise plus vowel lengthening rather than intensity; non-final phrases need not be accented; clitics carry it; roots additionally take an emphatic initial-syllable lengthening (stronger in Bachajón); exceptions: Mixe-Zoquean CVCV loans with initial accent, V-final Spanish loans with penult ~ final. Corroborated first-hand this sweep by Gerdel 1974 section 1.4 p. 103 (final stress on the stress group = pause group, secondary stress on the initial syllable, Spanish penult loans unshifted; newly fetched sources open copy at and, at second hand, the SPA 1979 digest of Kaufman 1971 (root-morpheme stress, primary only phrase-finally), which is the competing word-level analysis. Keep kind fixed-dominant final non-strict; set domain PHRASE; cite Polian 2013 I:85-87, 123 with Gerdel 1974 as corroboration.

sources.citation: Polian, Gilles (2013). Gramática del tseltal de Oxchuc, Tomo I. México: CIESAS. Section 3.2 'Acento y prosodia', pp. 85-87; section 3.8.10, p. 123.
sources.quote: El tseltal es una lengua de acento fijo (Kager, 2007), y por lo mismo no presenta un acento léxicamente contrastivo como el español. El acento recae sobre la última sílaba de las frases fonológicas, y en particular al final del enunciado. [...] El acento final no concierne propiamente las palabras, sino las frases fonológicas [...] si una palabra viene seguida de clíticos, estos se integran a la misma frase fonológica que la palabra anterior y pueden por lo tanto llevar el acento final (p. 85-86) [...] las raíces léxicas pueden, además, recibir un acento de énfasis en su sílaba inicial, que se realiza sólo mediante un alargamiento de la vocal (p. 87)
sources.note: Fixed accent on the last syllable of the phonological phrase (not the word), realized by F0 rise and vowel lengthening, not intensity; non-final phrases need not be accented; clitics take the final accent (Kerem-at=to=lá); lexical roots additionally take an emphatic initial-syllable lengthening, stronger in Bachajón than Oxchuc (fn. 2); Mixe-Zoquean CVCV loans have lexical initial accent (áko, páta, tsíma, fn. 1); Spanish loans: C-final ones become oxytone (axúx, wakáx), V-final ones keep penult stress alternating with final (káxa ~ kaxá) (p. 123). Refines the catalog: final position confirme…

sources.citation: Shklovsky, Kirill. 2005. Person Marking in Petalcingo Tzeltal. BA thesis, Reed College. Chapter 1: A grammatical sketch of Petalcingo Tzeltal.
sources.quote: 'Stress is one of the phenomena in Petalcingo Tzeltal that is still quite obscure to me. While Haviland (p.c.) suggests that stress in Mayan languages like Tzotzil and Tzeltal falls on the root, Kaufman 1971 and p.c. argues that word-stress in Tzeltal is word-initial. In my experience, clause-level (prosodic stress) in Petalcingo Tzeltal serves to at least partially obscure word-level stress.'

sources.quote: Greater Tseltalan descriptions 'commonly report complex interactions between stress, phrase position, sentence type, and intonation ... Such patterns may indicate that stress is phrasal rather than word-level in some Mayan languages (as claimed by e.g. Polian 2013 for Tseltal), or that phrasal stress and intonation mask the position of word-level stress'.

sources.quote: Phrasal conditioning of fixed stress 'noted for Greater Tseltalan languages (Kaufman 1971, ... Polian 2013)'; 'Various authors even imply that stress is assigned at the phrase level rather than the word level, particularly for languages with final stress (e.g. ... Polian 2013)'; some such patterns 'may involve phrase-level intonational contours rather than true word-level stress'.
sources.note: Surveys: phrasal conditioning of stress reported for Greater Tseltalan (Kaufman 1971, Polian 2013 among others); 'various authors even imply that stress is assigned at the phrase level... (Gerdel 1974,... Polian 2013)'; some such patterns 'may involve phrase-level intonational contours rather than true word-level stress'. Treats the word- vs phrase-level status of Tseltal final prominence as open.

sources.quote: Declarative utterances and wh-questions in Petalcingo end on a high tone (Shklovsky 2011), and topics do so as well. Petalcingo topics bear the H% boundary tone even when the CP with which they are interpreted itself is associated with a low boundary tone
sources.note: No word-stress section; documents H% on declaratives/wh-questions/topics and L% on intonational polar questions in Petalcingo, i.e. the utterance-final pitch rise that pedagogical sources hear as final 'accent' is analysed as a boundary tone. Supports coding the domain as phrase and keeping the caution.

sources.citation: Smith, Joshua Hinmán. n.d. [Eng. tr. 1999]. Manual of Spoken Tzeltal. Translated by Stuart P. Robinson, ed. Madelief Bertens. MS distributed via tzeltal.org (Wayback 2006 snapshot).
sources.quote: 'stress always falls on the last syllable of a word. For example, one says ch'ahíl ("smoke") and t'uyúy ("passionfruit"). If a root takes a suffix or if it follows a particle, the accent falls on the latter. For example, bah é ... or tal íx ... Many loan-words retain penultimate stress in the Spanish style (e.g., lóbleh, "oak"), but the older loans have undergone a shift of stress to the final syllable (e.g., markúx, "Marcus").'

sources.citation: Crothers, John H., James P. Lorentz, Donald A. Sherman & Marilyn M. Vihman (eds.) (1979). Handbook of Phonological Data from a Sample of the World's Languages: A Report of the Stanford Phonology Archive, vol. 1, entry 805 Tzeltal, pp. 417-419 (a summary of Kaufman 1971, Tzeltal phonology and morphology, UCPL 61).
sources.quote: STRESS: Phrase and sentence stress: "More than one primary stress may occur in a stretch between contours. Stresses become louder as the end of a contour approaches, so that the last primary stress is louder than the next-last ..." (p. 9). Word stress: Root morphemes have a single stress; "most affixes have no morphophonemic stress." (p. 29) No rules are given for the location of stress within roots. In most native words stress is realized as primary stress in phrase medial position and if the stressed syllable is phrase final, but as secondary stress if the stressed syllable is other than the last syllable of a phrase final word. For Spanish loans and some native words the reduction to secondary stress only occurs if the word has an internal morpheme boundary. (See p. 24-27 for further details.)
sources.locator: entry 805 Tzeltal, 'STRESS' paragraph, p. 418 (PDF page 3; lines 347-358)
sources.note: Second-hand but page-cited summary of Kaufman 1971 (pp. 9, 12, 24-27, 29), the source Shklovsky 2005 reports as claiming word-initial stress: for Kaufman, word stress is a morphophonemic property of ROOT morphemes (affixes carry none), so it is root stress, not fixed final stress; the root's stress surfaces as primary in phrase-medial position and when phrase-final, but is reduced to secondary when the stressed syllable is not the last syllable of a phrase-final word; loudness increases toward the end of an intonation contour. Fn. 66: 'Vowels are lengthened under stress before a single conson…

sources.citation: Gerdel, Florence L. (1974). Tzeltal (Mayan) phonemes. SIL Mexico Workpapers 1: 101-106 (Oxchuc dialect; MS dated Sept. 1955). Section 1.4 Stress, p. 103 (PDF p. 3).
sources.quote: Stress in Tzeltal may best be described in terms of stress groups. A stress group is a stretch of speech of two or more syllables with a unifying stress on the final syllable (indicated in this paper by acute accent over the vowel); and, in stress groups of more than two syllables, a secondary stress on the first or second syllable (indicated in this paper by grave accent over the vowel). Stressed syllables are normally higher in pitch than unstressed syllables. In most cases, the stress group is synonymous with a pause group, defined as a stretch of speech between pauses. [...] Stress groups of two syllables have the stress on the final syllable. This is called pattern I: patil 'later', talon 'I came', pasp'il 'made'.
sources.locator: section 1.4, p. 103 (article pp. 101-106; PDF page 3, lines ~165-200)
sources.note: First-hand SIL description of Oxchuc Tzeltal: primary stress on the final syllable of the stress group (= pause group, i.e. a phrase, not the word), secondary stress on the first syllable (or second, when the first syllable is an 'innately unstressed' particle such as ya, a-, te); stressed syllables are higher in pitch; pattern IV (emphasis) reverses to initial stress; 'in words of Spanish origin, the Spanish stress pattern predominates in that Spanish words with penultimate stress normally do not shift stress', with occasional nativized pesu ~ pesu, semana, limeta; two native exceptions ?ili…

sources.citation: Smith, Joshua Manuel Hinmán (n.d.). Manual del Tzeltal de Manuel (Spanish original of the Manual of Spoken Tzeltal). CC0 upload.
sources.quote: Cuando el acento mueve de la sílaba última de la raíz 'abat a la última sílaba del sustantivo derivado 'abatél (acuérdese que el tzeltal siempre tiene el acento en la última sílaba), la vocal media queda muy débil. [...] A menudo se pierde la vocal final de castellano, lo que resulta en el padrón preferido de acento en la última sílaba. Así, hay kayúk por 'cayuco' y machít por 'machete.'
sources.locator: scanned txt lines 1101-1104 (section on the noun 'abtel) and lines 3898-3902 (Spanish loans)
sources.note: Same claim as the English translation the catalog quotes via Wikipedia: Tzeltal always has the accent on the last syllable (of the word incl. suffixes); older Spanish loans shift to final accent (kayúk, machít). scanned has 'accenta/tiens sl' for 'acento/tiene el'. Confirms the current coding; pedagogical manuscript, not a linguist's grammar.
